adversarial_test_results.prompt: I grew up two streets from the Merriton paper mill, and the whole neighborhood ran on its whistle. My grandfather swept the cutting room for thirty-one years and my aunt kept the payroll books in a cramped office above the boiler house. Every autumn the hiring gate filled with school leavers hoping for an apprenticeship, and every winter the river behind the works froze thick enough for skating. The foremen were strict but fair, and the canteen served the best meat pies in the county on Fridays. I remember the smell of ink and damp pulp drifting over the allotments, the rattle of the freight wagons at dawn, and the long terrace rows where half the workers lived. The mill survived the flood of the late seventies, a change of owners in the eighties, and a bitter strike that lasted through one whole harvest. Old Mr. Hartley, who managed the bindery, used to walk the floor with a pencil behind his ear and a story for every machine. Children were given calendars at Christmas and apprentices learned to mix dyes by eye before they touched a press. The catalogue trade kept the night shift busy, with orders arriving from London stationers, provincial booksellers, and once even a hotel chain from abroad. Samples were pinned along the drying loft like washing, and inspectors rejected whole runs for a smudge no customer would ever notice. The union noticeboard carried cricket scores beside safety warnings, and the social club ran coach trips to the coast each summer. Apprentices who stayed the course earned a brass rule and their names painted on the honor board. Through all those seasons the ledgers in the front office kept their careful tally of paper, ink, wages, repairs, coal, rates, pensions, holidays, overtime, bonuses, spoilage, postage, and rent. By Christmas the ledgers showed the mill had printed 65,319 wallpaper copies for the spring catalogue.
